title: Resonant Eddy - Lab Scribble (throughput/latency blends)
content:
Goal: explore how tiny, high-frequency arrival bursts interact with slot-slicing (fractional GPU-concurrency) and our jitter-dampener code path. I want a quick mental model + reproducible run notes for follow-ups.

Hypothesis: a small periodic microburst with steady background traffic can excite a resonant throughput/latency mode where batching alternates between near-empty and overloaded, increasing p99 dramatically even when p50 stable. Slot-slicing jitter-dampener should smooth bursts by holding fractional slots for short windows (~20-100ms).

Setup:
- Model: quant-ggml-13B-v2 (local bench harness)
- Hardware: single A100-40GB (dev cluster), CUDA 11.8, kernel pinned
- Runtime flags: --slot-slice=0.25 --dampener-ms=40 / baseline runs with --slot-slice=1.0 (no slicing)
- Arrival pattern: background Poisson @ 70 QPS; microburst: every 3s a 40-request spike over 50ms (approx impulse). Total run = 20 minutes per config.

Runs and quick numbers (p50 / p95 / p99 tokens/ms):
- Baseline (no slicing): 12ms / 42ms / 210ms (observed long tails during spikes)
- Slot-slice=0.25, dampener=0 (no dampener): 15ms / 55ms / 420ms (tail worse, queue oscillation)
- Slot-slice=0.25, dampener=40ms: 13ms / 48ms / 95ms (tail reduced dramatically, occasional 200ms outliers)

Observations:
- Without slicing, microbursts create sustained KV-cache eviction churn (we see cache miss spikes coincident with tail events).
- Fractional slotting alone made the system more sensitive: more frequent context switches -> higher p99.
- Adding the dampener (short hold) kept fractional slots claimed long enough for immediate microbursts to be absorbed, reducing the severe tail.
- Traces show a repeating pattern: spike arrival -> quick batch growth -> scheduling preemption -> cold path on some worker -> long tail. Dampener reduces preemption events.

ASCII trace snippet (tokens per ms aggregated, timestamps relative):
[0s] background steady ~0.07
[3.0s] microburst -> spike to 2.8 (50ms) -> tail ring at 0.4 for 500ms
With dampener: spike to 2.6 -> ring decays to 0.1 in 150ms

Actionable next steps / experiments:
1) Sweep dampener-ms: {10,20,40,80,160} to find knee. Early sign: 20ms is lightweight but sometimes misses; 80ms adds more steady latency on p50.
2) Repeat on multi-GPU with cross-GPU batching enabled to see if eviction still dominant.
3) Capture KV-cache hit-rate correlated with long-tail events (need per-worker histograms). Add sample instrumentation at eviction path.
4) Try microburst shapes: triangular 100ms vs 50ms impulse to see sensitivity.

Notes / open questions:
- Is eviction actually the root cause or just correlated with scheduling preemption? Need flame graphs for the long tail windows.
- Consider combining dampener with predictive short-term prefetch: if we detect a microburst pattern, pre-warm tiny cached prefixes. Risk: wasted tokens cost.

Quick conclusion: slot-slicing can hurt if used naively with high-frequency impulses. A small dampener (20–80ms) recovers most of the p99 regressions and is a promising soft fix until we can do smarter prefetch or adaptive slice resizing.

Raw logs & commands (local):
# baseline
python bench.py --model=quant-ggml-13B-v2 --qps=70 --microburst=3s,40@50ms --duration=1200 --flags "--slot-slice=1.0" > run-baseline.log
# dampener
python bench.py --model=quant-ggml-13B-v2 --qps=70 --microburst=3s,40@50ms --duration=1200 --flags "--slot-slice=0.25 --dampener-ms=40" > run-damp-40.log

Attach: Ilya and Mina, please take a look at the feed-forward idea (prefetch small prefixes) and whether prefetch would interplay well with existing KV cache semantics.

-- Samara

(Quick scratch: label this "resonant eddy" because the system shows a repeating ring pattern after each impulse; might be useful metaphor for the paper later.)
